churn_resistance.rationale: The data layer is genuinely well-isolated (one seam for the API, one for formatting), so the likeliest requirement change — the API moving — touches few files. But the framework's own next step (Cache Components default in 17) invalidates a config export copy-pasted into six pages plus a hand-rolled caching module, and there are no types at the API boundary to catch shape changes early.

findings.issue: `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` is repeated in six page files; this segment config is removed when Cache Components is enabled (Next 16 docs) and Cache Components becomes the default in Next 17, so every route needs editing at the next major upgrade. It is also redundant given `fetch(..., { cache: 'no-store' })` already opts these routes out of caching.
findings.suggestion: Adopt `cacheComponents: true` + `partialPrefetching: true` in next.config.mjs and drop the per-page `dynamic` exports, using `'use cache'`/`cacheLife` where a shelf is wanted. At minimum centralize the decision instead of copy-pasting it per page.

findings.issue: Hand-rolled globalThis promise cache duplicates the framework's current caching machinery and has no lifetime, so stale species data persists for the process lifetime even though the spec calls the API a live service.
findings.suggestion: Replace with `'use cache'` + `cacheLife(...)` on the data functions once cacheComponents is enabled; that gives the same in-memory behaviour with a framework-managed lifetime.

findings.issue: No types at the API boundary: raw response shapes (`varieties`, `damage_relations`, `effect_entries`, `flavor_text_entries`) are consumed inline in six page components, so an API shape change ripples through the UI instead of surfacing in one place.
findings.suggestion: Add JSDoc or TypeScript types for the objects returned by lib/data.js and lib/api.js so pages program against a typed contract, keeping PokeAPI shape knowledge inside lib/.

findings.issue: Reads `window.location.search` and rebuilds the query by hand instead of using `useSearchParams` from next/navigation, mixing browser globals with the framework router (and duplicating the query builder in app/app/page.jsx:12).
findings.suggestion: Use `useSearchParams()` and share one query-building helper between the server pagination links and the client controls.

findings.issue: URL assembled with a template literal (`?game=${e.target.value}#moves`) without encoding, inconsistent with the URLSearchParams-based builders elsewhere.
findings.suggestion: Build with URLSearchParams and append '#moves', so the pattern stays safe if version-group names ever change.

findings.issue: Hardcodes the media path pattern `/media/sprites/pokemon/<id>.png` outside the data layer instead of using the `sprites.front_default` field the API provides, so media-layout knowledge lives in a UI component.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the sprite URL in lib/data.js (from the API's sprite field or the documented pattern) and pass it to the card as data.

findings.issue: No loading.jsx or Suspense boundaries anywhere: every route renders fully server-side before responding, so client-side navigations block on the whole data fetch and the app cannot benefit from the current streaming/partial-prerender model.
findings.suggestion: Add a route-level loading.jsx (or wrap slow sections in Suspense) so a shell streams immediately while data loads — the shape Cache Components assumes.

summary: This is current-generation code on the latest stable Next (16.4.3): async params, next/navigation hooks, generateMetadata, top-level Turbopack config, three dependencies total, and a genuinely well-fenced data layer that makes an API change cheap. The main thing that will age is the caching model — six copy-pasted `force-dynamic` exports plus a hand-rolled globalThis cache sit on the pre-16.4 model that the current release recommends replacing and Next 17 makes the default. Untyped API responses across six pages are the second churn vector. I'd merge it and file a follow-up to adopt Cache Components and add boundary types.
